posts.title: Taobao vs 1688: Which Platform Is Right for You?
posts.excerpt: Taobao and 1688 are both Alibaba-owned platforms, but they serve different buyers. Learn when to use each one as an international purchaser.
posts.author: BuyTCN Editorial Team
posts.content:
Choosing Between Taobao and 1688: A Practical Guide for International Buyers

If you're sourcing products from China, you've likely run into both Taobao and 1688. Both are massive marketplaces owned by Alibaba Group, but they serve very different purposes. Understanding the gap between them can save you time, money, and a lot of headaches.

Here's what international buyers need to know before picking one—or deciding to use both.

What Is Taobao?

Taobao is a consumer-facing marketplace, similar to Amazon or eBay. It's where everyday shoppers in China browse and buy everything from clothing and electronics to home goods and hobby supplies. The platform is designed for individual buyers, with product pages that include photos, descriptions, reviews, and chat-based communication with sellers.

For international buyers, Taobao is generally more approachable. Many sellers list in Chinese, but the interface has improved over the years, and there are more third-party tools and agents that support Taobao purchases than 1688. If you're buying small quantities or single items for personal use or product testing, Taobao is usually the easier starting point.

What Is 1688?

1688.com is Alibaba's domestic wholesale platform. It's where Chinese businesses go to source products in bulk from factories and distributors. The platform is geared toward B2B transactions, with pricing that reflects wholesale margins, minimum order quantities, and direct factory relationships.

The trade-off is accessibility. 1688 is almost entirely in Chinese, sellers typically expect bulk orders, and the platform isn't built for international buyers. You'll need an agent or a sourcing partner to navigate it effectively. But the upside is real: prices on 1688 are often significantly lower than Taobao because you're cutting out the retail layer.

Key Differences at a Glance

  • Target buyer: Taobao serves individual consumers; 1688 serves businesses and wholesalers.
  • Pricing: Taobao prices are retail. 1688 prices are wholesale, often 20–50% lower on comparable items.
  • Minimum order quantity: Taobao usually allows single-unit purchases. 1688 often requires minimums of 10, 50, or more units.
  • Language: Taobao has more third-party support for non-Chinese speakers. 1688 is firmly Chinese-first.
  • Product variety: Both platforms carry enormous selections, but 1688 tends to have more factory-direct and private-label options.
  • Payment and shipping: Taobao accepts more familiar payment methods. 1688 transactions are structured for domestic Chinese payment systems.

When to Use Taobao

Taobao makes sense when you're in the early stages of sourcing. If you're evaluating product ideas, ordering samples, or buying small batches for testing, the lower commitment and easier navigation are worth the higher per-unit cost. It's also the better choice if you need a wide variety of niche or lifestyle products that aren't typically sold through wholesale channels.

Many new importers start on Taobao to validate demand before committing to larger orders. That's a smart approach, and it's exactly why learning how to buy from Taobao in the USA is one of the first steps for US-based buyers entering the China sourcing space.

When to Use 1688

2026 Guide for Small Importers" title="China Factory Sourcing Guide for Small Importers (2026)">When you've identified a product with proven demand and you're ready to scale, 1688 becomes the more economical choice. The lower prices compound quickly when you're ordering hundreds or thousands of units. Factories listed on 1688 are often the same ones supplying Taobao sellers—so you're getting closer to the source.

1688 is also the go-to platform if you're exploring private label manufacturing. Many factories on 1688 offer OEM and ODM services, meaning they can produce products under your brand. If you're serious about building a branded product line, private label manufacturing in China often starts with sourcing on 1688 rather than Taobao.

The Realistic Challenge: Language and Logistics

Neither Taobao nor 1688 is designed for direct international purchase. Sellers don't typically ship abroad, payment options are China-centric, and product listings can be dense with technical details in Mandarin. This is where a sourcing agent becomes valuable—not as a luxury, but as a practical necessity for most international buyers.

A reliable agent handles the language barrier, negotiates with sellers, consolidates orders from multiple suppliers, and arranges international shipping. For 1688 specifically, an agent is essentially required unless you're fluent in Chinese and familiar with domestic business practices. If you're considering this route, understanding what a 1688 agent does and when to use one can help you decide whether the investment makes sense for your order volume and goals.

How BuyTCN Can Help

At BuyTCN, we support buyers who source from both Taobao and 1688. Whether you're ordering a single sample or consolidating a multi-supplier shipment, our team handles purchasing, quality control, and logistics so you don't have to navigate these platforms alone. We provide QC photos before shipping so you can verify product quality before it leaves China, and we consolidate orders from multiple suppliers into one shipment to reduce shipping costs.

Which Should You Choose?

There's no single answer. Here's a practical framework:

  • Start with Taobao if you're testing products, buying samples, or ordering in small quantities.
  • Move to 1688 once you've validated a product and need wholesale pricing for larger orders.
  • Use both if different products or suppliers are better found on each platform.

The most successful international buyers don't treat this as an either-or decision. They use Taobao for exploration and 1688 for scale, often with an agent managing the process on their behalf.

Frequently Asked Questions

Can I buy directly from 1688 as an international buyer?

Technically yes, but practically it's very difficult. The platform is in Chinese, payment methods are designed for domestic buyers, and most sellers won't ship internationally. Using a sourcing agent is the standard approach for international buyers.

Are products on 1688 the same quality as Taobao?

Not necessarily. 1688 listings often describe the same products you'd find on Taobao, but at lower prices because they're positioned for bulk buyers. Quality can vary by supplier, which is why inspecting products before shipment—through QC photos or third-party inspection—is important regardless of which platform you use.

Is it worth paying more for Taobao to avoid the complexity of 1688?

It depends on your order volume. For small orders or samples, Taobao's convenience is worth the premium. But if you're ordering 100+ units of the same product, the price difference on 1688 can be substantial enough to justify the extra effort of working with an agent.

posts.title: Private Label Manufacturing in China: Getting Started
posts.excerpt: A practical guide to private label manufacturing in China for US buyers — from finding suppliers and vetting factories to QC, shipping, and common mistakes to avoid.
posts.author: BuyTCN Editorial Team
posts.content:
What Is Private Label Manufacturing in China?

Private label manufacturing in China means partnering with a Chinese factory to produce goods under your own brand name. The factory handles production based on your specifications — materials, sizing, packaging, labeling — and ships the finished product to you. You then sell it as your own brand.

This model powers everything from skincare and pet supplies to electronics and home goods. It's how many US brands scale without owning a factory. The key is finding the right manufacturer and managing the process carefully.

Why US Buyers Choose China for Private Label Production

China remains one of the most practical destinations for private label manufacturing, especially for small and mid-size US businesses. The main reasons:

  • Cost efficiency: Labor and material costs are generally lower than in North America or Europe, especially at scale.
  • Manufacturing depth: China has mature supply chains across nearly every product category — from textiles to electronics to cosmetics packaging.
  • MOQ flexibility: Many factories now work with smaller minimum order quantities, making it accessible for startups.
  • Experience with export: Established factories understand US labeling requirements, safety standards, and shipping logistics.

That said, success depends on due diligence. Not every factory that claims to do private label work has the quality control, communication, or reliability you need.

Step 1: Define Your Product and Specifications

Before you contact any manufacturer, get clear on what you're building. Vague requests lead to vague results. Prepare the following:

  • Product specs: Materials, dimensions, weight, colors, packaging requirements
  • Target price point: Your landed cost goal per unit (including shipping and duties)
  • Order volume: Initial order size and expected reorder frequency
  • Compliance needs: Any certifications required (FDA, CPC, CE, etc.)
  • Branding assets: Logo files, packaging design, label templates

The more detail you provide upfront, the more accurate the quotes you'll receive — and the fewer surprises down the line.

Step 2: Find and Vet Potential Manufacturers

There are several channels for finding private label manufacturers in China:

  • Alibaba and Global Sources: Good for initial research and comparing multiple suppliers. Look for verified suppliers with trade history and reviews.
  • 1688.com: China's domestic B2B platform often has lower prices and more factories willing to do private label work. This is where many experienced sourcing agents find their suppliers.
  • Trade shows: Canton Fair, Yiwu Fair, and category-specific exhibitions let you meet manufacturers in person and see product samples.
  • Referrals: Other US importers in your niche can point you toward factories they've worked with successfully.

Once you have a shortlist, vet each factory thoroughly. Check their business license, export experience, and whether they hold relevant certifications for your product category. Request samples before committing to any order. Our guide on finding reliable Chinese suppliers covers vetting in more detail.

Red Flags to Watch For

  • Reluctance to share factory photos or videos
  • No samples available or unwilling to charge for them
  • Vague answers about MOQs, lead times, or payment terms
  • No experience exporting to the US
  • Prices that seem too good to be true

Step 3: Negotiate Terms and Place the Trial Order

When you find a suitable manufacturer, negotiate the key terms before signing anything:

  • MOQ: Confirm the minimum order quantity and whether it's negotiable for a first order.
  • Unit pricing: Get a detailed quote that breaks down material, labor, packaging, and tooling costs.
  • Sample cost and lead time: Samples should be approved before full production starts.
  • Payment terms: Typical terms are 30% deposit and 70% before shipment. Avoid factories demanding 100% upfront.
  • Quality standards: Define acceptable tolerances, defect rates, and inspection criteria in writing.
  • Lead time: Get a realistic production timeline and build in buffer for delays.
  • IP protection: If your design or branding is unique, discuss how the factory will protect it.

Start with a smaller trial order before scaling up. This lets you validate quality, communication, and reliability without a large financial commitment.

Step 4: Manage Quality Control

Quality control is where many new private label buyers make costly mistakes. Never assume the factory's internal QC is sufficient — you need your own verification step.

At a minimum, request pre-shipment photos or videos of the finished goods. A third-party inspection service can also visit the factory before payment is released. This is especially important for your first few orders when you're still building the relationship.

BuyTCN offers agent purchasing and QC photo services that can help verify product quality before goods leave the factory, giving you an extra layer of confidence.

Step 5: Handle Shipping and Customs

Once your order passes quality checks, you'll need to arrange logistics. Options include:

  • Sea freight: Most cost-effective for large orders. Transit time is typically 30–45 days to the US West Coast.
  • Air freight: Faster (5–10 days) but significantly more expensive per unit.
  • Express courier: Best for small sample shipments or urgent restocks.

Make sure your manufacturer provides the correct documentation — commercial invoice, packing list, bill of lading, and any certificates required for your product category. If you're consolidating orders from multiple factories, a sourcing agent can handle consolidation and shipping logistics more efficiently than managing each factory separately.

Common Mistakes to Avoid

  • Skipping samples: Never place a full order without approving a physical sample first.
  • Underestimating lead times: Factories often run behind schedule. Plan for delays, especially during Chinese holidays.
  • Poor communication: Use clear written specs and confirm understanding. Assume nothing.
  • Ignoring compliance: Some products require specific certifications for US sale. Know your requirements before ordering.
  • Going with the cheapest quote: The lowest price often means corner-cutting on materials or QC.

When to Work with a Sourcing Agent

Some buyers handle private label manufacturing directly. Others find that a sourcing agent makes the process smoother — especially for first-time importers. An agent can help with supplier vetting, negotiation, sample coordination, quality inspections, and shipping consolidation.

If you're placing your first private label order or working with factories on 1688 that don't speak English, a sourcing agent can reduce risk and save time. The investment typically pays for itself by avoiding costly mistakes on material, quality, or shipping.

Getting Started: A Quick Checklist

  • Define your product specs and target price
  • Research and shortlist 3–5 manufacturers
  • Request and evaluate samples
  • Negotiate terms in writing
  • Place a trial order
  • Arrange QC verification before shipment
  • Plan logistics and customs documentation
  • Evaluate the results and decide on scaling

Private label manufacturing in China is a proven path to building your own brand — but it requires preparation, patience, and attention to detail. Start small, learn from each order, and build your supplier relationships over time.

Frequently Asked Questions

What is the typical MOQ for private label manufacturing in China?

MOQs vary widely by product category and factory. Some factories accept orders as low as 50–100 units, while others require 500–1,000 or more. It's worth asking about MOQ flexibility, especially for your first order. Many factories will negotiate for a trial order even if their standard MOQ is higher.

How long does private label production take?

Production timelines depend on product complexity, order size, and factory workload. A typical range is 20–45 days for production, plus shipping time. Always confirm lead times with your factory and build in buffer for delays, especially around Chinese holidays like Chinese New Year.

Do I need a US import license to private label from China?

You don't need a special import license to bring goods into the US as a private label buyer. However, you will need an EIN (Employer Identification Number) for customs purposes, and certain product categories require specific certifications or registrations (e.g., FDA for cosmetics and food-contact items, CPC for children's products). Work with a customs broker if you're unsure about your product's requirements.

How do I protect my brand and designs in China?

Register your trademark in China through the China Trademark Office before sharing your branding with any factory. Consider signing a non-disclosure agreement (NDA) and a manufacturing contract that includes IP protection clauses. While enforcement can be challenging, having legal documentation in place is a important step.

posts.title: China Factory Sourcing Guide for Small Importers (2026)
posts.excerpt: A practical factory sourcing guide for small importers: how to find, evaluate, and build reliable relationships with Chinese manufacturers — without the common pitfalls.
posts.author: BuyTCN Editorial Team
posts.content:
Why Factory Sourcing Matters for Small Importers

Buying directly from a factory in China can be the difference between thin margins and a sustainable import business. When you source from a manufacturer instead of a trading company, you typically get better unit pricing, more control over specifications, and the ability to build a long-term supply relationship. For small importers, those advantages compound quickly.

The challenge isn't that factory sourcing is impossible—it's that it requires a different approach than ordering from a platform like Alibaba. Factories speak a different language, operate on different timelines, and often have minimum order quantities that feel intimidating at first. This guide walks through the practical steps small importers can take to source directly from Chinese factories without getting burned.

How to Identify the Right Factory

Start with the right search channels

Factory sourcing begins with knowing where factories actually list their capabilities. The major B2B marketplaces are useful, but they aggregate both factories and trading companies. To separate the two, look for these signals:

  • Factory audits and verification badges — Third-party inspection reports and on-site verification carry more weight than self-reported claims.
  • Product focus — Factories that specialize in one category or material tend to have deeper expertise than generalists.
  • Production photos and videos — Real factory floor imagery, especially showing active production lines, is harder to fake than a polished brochure.
  • Business license details — A Chinese business license will list the company's registered scope of business. If it includes manufacturing terms rather than just trading or wholesale, that's a positive sign.

Use industry directories and trade shows

Beyond online platforms, industry-specific directories and trade shows remain some of the most reliable ways to find factories. Canton Fair, Yiwu Fair, and regional trade exhibitions in manufacturing hubs like Shenzhen, Dongguan, and Ningbo connect buyers directly with producers. Even virtual trade shows and industry association directories can surface factories that don't advertise heavily online.

Evaluating Factory Capability

Once you've identified potential factories, the next step is assessing whether they can actually deliver what you need. Small importers often skip this step and jump straight to requesting a quote, which is where problems start.

Request a detailed quotation

A professional factory quotation should include unit pricing at different volume tiers, tooling or setup fees, sample costs, estimated lead times, and payment terms. If a factory provides a vague quote with no breakdown, treat that as a red flag. Clear pricing shows they understand the product and have experience working with international buyers.

Ask about their experience with your product type

Not all factories are created equal, even within the same category. A factory that has produced for Western brands will understand quality expectations, documentation requirements, and communication norms that a factory serving only the domestic Chinese market may not. Ask specifically about overseas clients, export experience, and any certifications relevant to your product category.

Order a sample before committing

Never place a production order without evaluating a physical sample. Samples reveal material quality, construction standards, and how well the factory communicates during the sampling process. Pay attention to response time, willingness to revise, and whether the sample matches the quoted specifications. A factory that rushes samples or ignores feedback is unlikely to perform better on a full order.

Negotiating MOQ and Pricing

Minimum order quantities are one of the biggest barriers for small importers. Factories often set MOQs based on their production line efficiency — running a smaller batch means more changeover time and higher per-unit cost. Here's how to work within that reality.

  • Ask for a tiered pricing schedule — Many factories will lower the MOQ if you accept a higher per-unit price at the lower tier.
  • Consolidate orders over time — Some factories allow you to build an order across multiple production runs, especially if you establish a recurring relationship.
  • Consider shared production — In some cases, factories will run your product alongside similar items to meet minimum run requirements, which can reduce your cost.
  • Be realistic about your numbers — Factories can sense when a buyer is guessing at demand. Honest conversations about your sales projections help them find a workable solution.

Quality Control Before Shipping

Quality control is where many small importers make costly mistakes. Shipping a full container based on a sample or a photo can lead to significant losses if the production run doesn't match expectations. A practical approach includes:

  • Pre-production samples — Approve a sample made from the actual production materials before the factory begins manufacturing.
  • During-production inspections — For larger orders, request photos or videos from the factory at key production milestones.
  • Final random inspection — Before shipment, have a third-party inspector or agent check a random sample of the finished goods against your specification sheet.

Services like BuyTCN offer quality control photo verification before goods are shipped, which gives small importers a practical way to catch issues without hiring a full inspection service for every order.

Building a Reliable Sourcing Workflow

Factory sourcing isn't a one-time event — it's a process that improves with each order. Successful small importers tend to follow a consistent workflow:

  1. Research and shortlist factories
  2. Request and compare quotations
  3. Order and evaluate samples
  4. Negotiate terms and place the order
  5. Monitor production and request progress updates
  6. Conduct quality checks before shipment
  7. Arrange shipping and customs clearance
  8. Review the order and document lessons learned

Each completed order should feed back into your process. Track which factories were responsive, which had quality issues, and what communication gaps caused delays. Over time, this builds a reliable supplier network that makes future sourcing faster and less risky.

When to Use a Sourcing Agent

Not every small importer needs a sourcing agent, but there are situations where one adds clear value. If you're new to China factory sourcing, don't speak Mandarin, or need to place orders across multiple factories, an agent can handle communication, quality checks, and logistics coordination. BuyTCN provides purchasing agent services for Taobao, 1688, and PDD, along with consolidation and worldwide shipping — useful for importers who want to start small and scale gradually.

Key Takeaways

  • Factory sourcing offers better pricing and control but requires more due diligence than marketplace purchasing.
  • Identify factories through verified listings, industry directories, and trade shows — not just marketplace search results.
  • Always order samples and evaluate quality before committing to a production run.
  • MOQs are negotiable, especially when you're transparent about your volume and growth plans.
  • Quality control at multiple stages protects you from costly shipping mistakes.
  • A consistent sourcing workflow improves with every order and reduces risk over time.

posts.title: What Is a 1688 Agent and When to Use One
posts.excerpt: Learn what a 1688 agent does, when it makes sense to use one, and how it can help US buyers access China's lowest wholesale prices.
posts.author: BuyTCN Editorial Team
posts.content:
What Is a 1688 Agent?

1688.com is Alibaba Group's domestic wholesale platform, aimed at Chinese buyers and businesses. It's where thousands of factories and trading companies list products at prices most US importers never see — often 30% to 60% lower than what's available on Alibaba.com or Amazon. But there's a catch: the site is almost entirely in Chinese, most suppliers don't speak English, payment is tied to Chinese bank accounts and Alipay, and shipping is arranged domestically within China.

That's where a 1688 agent comes in. An agent acts as your on-the-ground purchasing representative. You tell them what you want, they handle communication with the supplier, place the order, receive the goods at a warehouse in China, and then arrange international shipping to you. They bridge the language, payment, logistics, and quality-control gaps that make 1688 nearly impossible to navigate on your own.

What a 1688 Agent Actually Does

Product Sourcing and Supplier Vetting

A good agent doesn't just place orders — they help you find the right supplier in the first place. You might send a product image, a spec sheet, or even just a description of what you need. The agent searches 1688, compares listings, checks supplier ratings and transaction history, and recommends the best options. This is especially valuable because 1688 has tens of millions of listings, and the quality bar varies wildly from one factory to the next.

Communication and Negotiation

Suppliers on 1688 communicate in Chinese. They negotiate in Chinese yuan, discuss minimum order quantities, and handle custom specifications through WeChat or Alibaba's messaging system. An agent translates all of that — not just the language, but the business context. They clarify MOQs, negotiate pricing, confirm material specs, and make sure both sides understand exactly what's being ordered.

Purchase Execution and Payment

1688 orders typically require payment through Alipay or a Chinese bank transfer. Most international buyers don't have access to either. An agent handles the entire payment process on your behalf, using their own accounts and relationships with suppliers. You pay the agent in your currency, and they settle with the supplier in yuan.

Quality Control and Consolidation

Before goods ship internationally, a reliable agent inspects them. This usually means taking photos of each item, checking for defects, verifying quantities, and confirming that what arrived matches what you ordered. If something is wrong, the agent can request a replacement or refund from the supplier before anything leaves China. Multiple orders from different suppliers can also be consolidated into a single shipment, which dramatically reduces per-unit shipping costs.

When to Use a 1688 Agent

Not every buyer needs an agent, but there are clear situations where one makes the difference between a smooth sourcing experience and a costly mistake.

You're Sourcing in Bulk or Running a Business

If you're buying 50 units or more — whether for resale, private label, or internal use — an agent pays for itself. The savings on product cost alone usually outweigh the service fee, and the quality-control step prevents you from receiving a container full of defective goods. For ongoing orders, an agent becomes even more valuable because they build relationships with suppliers and can track consistency across multiple purchases.

You're Sourcing Products Not Found on Alibaba or Amazon

Many manufacturers list on 1688 but not on Alibaba.com. Some products simply don't exist on Western platforms. If you've been searching for a specific component, material, or style and can't find it elsewhere, 1688 is often the only place it exists — and an agent is your only practical way to access it.

You Want Lower Unit Costs Than Alibaba Offers

1688 prices are wholesale prices for the Chinese domestic market. Alibaba.com prices are marked up for international buyers. If your target landed cost isn't working with Alibaba suppliers, 1688 may offer a completely different price range. A comparison of 1688 vs Alibaba sourcing often shows 1688 winning on price for buyers who can navigate the platform.

You're Buying From Multiple Suppliers

Consolidation is one of the biggest practical advantages of using an agent. If you're sourcing from five different factories, shipping each order internationally on its own is expensive and inefficient. An agent receives all orders at a single warehouse, combines them into one shipment, and cuts your per-unit freight cost significantly. This is especially relevant if you're building a product line with components from different suppliers.

When a 1688 Agent May Not Be Worth It

There are scenarios where an agent adds less value. If you're placing a single small order for personal use, the service fees and minimum charges may eat into any savings. If the product you need is readily available on Alibaba with English-speaking support and trade assurance, the extra step of using an agent may not be necessary. And if you already have a trusted sourcing team in China, they may already be handling 1688 purchases directly.

How to Choose a 1688 Agent

Not all agents are equal. Here are a few things to look for:

  • Transparent pricing: Clear service fees with no hidden charges. You should know exactly what you're paying before you place an order.
  • QC photos before shipping: Every order should be inspected and photographed before it leaves the warehouse. If an agent ships without showing you the goods first, that's a red flag.
  • Consolidation capability: The ability to combine multiple orders into one shipment is essential for cost efficiency.
  • Experience with your product category: Some agents specialize in electronics, others in apparel or home goods. An agent familiar with your category will spot quality issues you might miss.
  • Responsive communication: Time zone differences are real, but a good agent responds within a reasonable window and keeps you updated at each step.

BuyTCN and 1688 Sourcing

At BuyTCN, we help US buyers source directly from 1688, Taobao, and PDD. Our 1688 agent purchasing service covers everything from supplier vetting and negotiation to order placement, quality inspection, and international shipping. Every order gets QC photos before it ships, and we consolidate multiple purchases into a single shipment to keep your costs down. If you're ready to explore what 1688 can offer, we make the process straightforward.

Bottom Line

A 1688 agent is a purchasing partner who handles the language, payment, logistics, and quality-control barriers that stand between US buyers and China's domestic wholesale market. If you're sourcing in volume, looking for products unavailable elsewhere, or trying to reduce unit costs below what Alibaba offers, an agent is not just convenient — it's essential. The right agent turns 1688 from an inaccessible Chinese website into a reliable supply chain channel.

posts.title: 1688 vs Alibaba: Which Is Better for Sourcing From China?
posts.excerpt: 1688 and Alibaba both sell Chinese products, but they serve very different buyers. Here is how to decide which one fits your order size, budget and needs.
posts.author: BuyTCN Editorial Team
posts.content:
1688 and Alibaba are both owned by Alibaba Group and both sell Chinese-made products. But they are built for different buyers, and choosing the wrong one wastes money.

The short version

1688 is China's domestic wholesale platform: Chinese-language, priced for the Chinese market, lower prices, smaller minimums on many items — but it expects Chinese payment, Chinese communication and shipping within China.

Alibaba.com is the export version: English-friendly, international payment and shipping built in, with higher prices that reflect export handling.

Price differences

For the same product, 1688 prices are often lower than Alibaba quotes for the same factory. Why? Alibaba sellers build export costs — English support, international logistics, payment processing and platform fees — into their prices. That does not mean Alibaba is overcharging; it means you are paying for services that make export easy.

If you can handle (or outsource) the China-side work, 1688 can be the cheaper route. If you need an out-of-the-box export experience, Alibaba is more straightforward.

Minimum order quantities

Alibaba sellers often expect larger minimum orders, especially for factory-direct pricing. 1688 has a wider spread — many items can be bought in small quantities because the platform serves domestic resellers and small shops. If you want a small first order, 1688 (via an agent) is frequently more flexible.

Language and support

Alibaba is English-first with trade assurance and dispute systems designed for international buyers. 1688 is entirely in Chinese, with no international buyer support. If you do not speak Chinese, you will either learn fast, use translation, or use a sourcing agent or 1688 agent to handle purchasing and seller communication.

Payment

Alibaba accepts international payment methods and holds funds via trade assurance on many transactions. 1688 expects Chinese payment (usually Alipay with a Chinese account). International buyers typically pay a 1688 agent, who purchases domestically on their behalf.

Quality control still applies to both

Neither platform guarantees product quality — sellers vary. The same verification rules apply: check the company, order samples, agree specifications in writing, and arrange inspection before shipment. A cheap supplier that ships a bad product is not a bargain.

So which should you use?

  • Small order, want lowest price, comfortable with an agent or Chinese platform: 1688 via a 1688 purchasing agent.
  • Need English support, trade assurance and international shipping handled for you: Alibaba.
  • Medium-volume repeat buying: compare both — suppliers on 1688 will sometimes quote export terms directly once you are established.

If you are unsure, send us the product you need and your quantity — we can check both platforms and show you the realistic comparison before you commit.

posts.title: How to Find Reliable Chinese Suppliers (2026 Guide)
posts.excerpt: Finding a reliable Chinese supplier is about verification, communication and quality control — not just a low quote. Here is a practical checklist for vetting suppliers and protecting your order.
posts.author: BuyTCN Editorial Team
posts.content:
Finding a supplier in China is easy. Finding a reliable one takes work. The difference usually comes down to verification, communication, samples and clear agreements — not the cheapest quote.

Start with the right sourcing channels

Different channels suit different buyers:

  • 1688 — Chinese wholesale platform, better for domestic-market quality and price, but designed for Chinese buyers; most suppliers expect Chinese payment and communication.
  • Alibaba / Made-in-China — built for export, English-friendly, but prices are often higher than the same factory would quote a domestic buyer.
  • Trade shows (Canton Fair) — useful for meeting suppliers in person, especially for larger orders.
  • Referrals and sourcing agents — a vetted agent who already works with suppliers can shorten the search considerably.

Verify before you trust

  • Ask for the supplier's business license and, where relevant, export license. For Chinese suppliers you can check company registration records yourself or ask your agent to.
  • Confirm they are a manufacturer, trader or agent — each changes risk and price. A trading company can still deliver well; just know who you are dealing with.
  • Check how long they have been operating and whether they have shipped similar products to your market.
  • Be suspicious of quotes far below every other supplier — unusually low prices usually mean lower quality, different materials or hidden costs.

Test with samples

Order samples before committing to a production run. Verify the sample matches the specification sheet you sent, not just what looks good in photos. For customized products, agree the exact materials, dimensions, colors, packaging and defect tolerance in writing before production starts.

Quality control is a process, not a promise

Between payment and shipment, a few checkpoints reduce risk:

  • Pre-production: confirm materials and components.
  • During production: for larger orders, consider a mid-production check.
  • Before shipment: inspect the finished goods — quantity, packaging, visible defects. If your supplier is far away or you cannot travel, an inspection service or an agent with QC capability can do this for you.

What a basic inspection can check: visible damage, wrong items, quantity discrepancies, obvious differences from the agreed specification, and packaging condition. It is not laboratory, technical or certification testing — know the difference.

Payment safety

For first orders, avoid paying 100% upfront to an unverified supplier. Common practice is a deposit (often 30%) with the balance tied to production milestones or before shipment. Use payment methods that give you some recourse, and always confirm the full breakdown — product cost, tooling, samples, QC and shipping — in writing before you pay.

What to do when it goes wrong

Even vetted suppliers make mistakes. Agree in advance how defects and delays are handled. If your order is inspected before shipment, problems are caught while they can still be fixed in China — which is far cheaper than shipping a bad batch and trying to return it internationally.

Whether you have a product spec or just an idea, a sourcing partner that manages the China-side work — supplier search, communication, purchasing, inspection and shipping — can make the difference between a painful first import and a repeatable one.

posts.title: How to Buy From Taobao in the USA (2026 Guide)
posts.excerpt: Taobao doesn't ship to the US or accept foreign cards. Here is a practical, step-by-step guide to buying from Taobao from the USA — what you need, what it costs, and the honest risks to know before you start.
posts.author: BuyTCN Editorial Team
posts.content:
Taobao is one of the largest consumer marketplaces in the world, and it offers products that are often hard to find in the United States. Buying from Taobao in the USA is not as simple as checking out on an American website.

Why Taobao is harder to buy from than a US site

Three things make a direct Taobao purchase difficult from the US:

  • No direct international shipping. Most Taobao sellers ship only within mainland China.
  • Chinese payments. Taobao checkout is built around Alipay and Chinese bank cards; foreign cards are generally not accepted.
  • Language and seller communication. Listings and disputes are in Chinese, and sellers typically do not handle international buyers.

None of these are reasons to give up — they just mean you need a method designed for international buyers.

Option 1: Use a Taobao agent (the most common route)

A Taobao agent handles the China-side work for you. You send the product link; the agent buys the item with a Chinese payment method, has it delivered to their China warehouse, and arranges international shipping to your address.

  1. You paste a Taobao product link and receive a quote with the item price, domestic shipping and estimated international shipping.
  2. You confirm and pay (agents usually accept PayPal or Wise).
  3. The agent purchases the item and it arrives at their China warehouse.
  4. For many orders the agent shares photos of the received item before shipping internationally.
  5. Your package ships with tracking, typically arriving in 7-15 days.

Good agents show you the real item cost and real freight receipt rather than hiding margin inside inflated numbers.

What does it actually cost?

  • Product price — usually close to Chinese retail, often below the US price for the same product.
  • China domestic shipping — a few yuan for delivery within China.
  • International shipping — depends on weight, dimensions, destination and line.

You should also account for possible customs duties, which depend on the product type, declared value and current de minimis rules — check the current rules rather than assuming.

Honest risks before you buy

  • Returns are difficult. Most Chinese sellers do not accept returns from overseas buyers.
  • Photos can differ from reality. If your agent shares warehouse photos before international shipping, that check can catch obvious problems first.
  • Customs and delays. Cross-border parcels can be held by customs.

How to choose a Taobao agent

  • Ask for a separate breakdown of item cost, domestic shipping, service fee and international shipping.
  • Prefer agents who share photos of the received item before shipping internationally.
  • Confirm payment methods and cancellation terms before you pay.
  • Check that they are a registered business.
